Editors' Introduction

Freud in 1910 warned against intrusion of countertransference and insisted that the analyst “recognize…and overcome it.” His ideas on the subject were interpreted by the psychoanalytic community as a caution against its appearance and use. Countertransference was something to be avoided and dismissed, an anathema to the analytic process. However, analysts beginning with Sandor Ferenczi and Helene Deutsch through D. W. Winnicott, Heinrich Racker, and others rethought its role and began to see the therapeutic value of countertransference. Hyman Spotnitz was also among those early pioneers who were investigating its function. In 1949 in a paper presented before the American Psychiatric Association he stated that the analyst “must be capable of feeling emotions induced by his patient and utilize these feelings to help the patient with his resistances.” This statement challenged the classical Freudian notions about countertransference. Through the continuing clinical work of Spotnitz and his colleagues at the Jewish Board of Guardians and through the work of other psychoanalysts, the concept of countertransference underwent considerable revision. Tremendous resistances had to be resolved, both on the professional and personal level. The findings generally met with skepticism within the psychoanalytic domain. On a personal level, the characterological resistances of the analyst were called into question due to the nature of the transference/countertransference matrix.

Editors' Introduction

It was from Clark University in 1909 that Sigmund Freud launched psychoanalysis in America. Freud's ideas were controversial, revolutionary, and ultimately to have a profound and enduring impact on how the development and functioning of the mind was to be understood and its pathology treated. Among Freud' most important discoveries was that of the transference process and the significance of the analyst's reactions to the patient as those reactions operate to hinder or faciliate analytic treatment. Since freud's time we have come to known much about countertransference, that is, the myriad responses which are stimulated within the analyst as a result of the analyst's presence to and interaction with the patient. We have also come to know that in the treatment of the more serious mental disorders, such as the borderline and narcissistanc conditions, the countertrsnsference process is highly complicated, emotionally and intellectually challenging, and often hazardous for both participants. Yet without recognition and constructive utilization of countertransference phenomena effective treatment cannot take place.

While we have learned much, many questions remain. To what extent, for example, must the analyst become a containeer for the patient's projections, that is, to what extent is it necessary in the analytic hour for the analyst to become the patient in order to under stand the patient's expereience. How exactly does this process take place? What is it about the process which is curative? What are the difficulties? To what extent does the analyst actively facilitate the process versus waiting for it to occur?

Carol Brod

Carol Brod

Carol Brod  

Freud, the pioneer explorer of the mysterious world of transference; Dora, the patient who illuminated both Freud's genius and his limitations; and turn-of-the-century Vienna, which produced and shaped this historically linked pair: these are the subjects of Hannah Decker's masterful psychological, historical, and sociological study.

This is the story of the problems and limitations that the treatment of Dora brought to light as Freud struggled with his own methodology, theory, and technique in the infant science of psychoanalysis. But it is also the story of Dora, and the society that contributed to her condition-Vienna, the extraordinary city where polyglot culture and social structure add contrast, shading, and illumination to the protagonists.

The author seeks to render Dora “an historical figure in her own right.” In this pursuit, she acquaints us with Dora's personal history and her reltionship to a world that seemed to promise her so much but in fact contributed to her illness, rage, and despair. The unsuccessful and unresourceful womanhood she attained was symptomatic of her being “a prisoner of her time in every way.”

Turn-of-the-century Vienna saw great movements of social change. Public attitudes were loosening toward Jews, women, education, and social opportunities for many who would have been shunned a generation earlier. The promise of these changes, however, was matched by the all-too-virulent backlashes that erupted against progress in all of these areas. For every advance in the European Jew's status, an anti-Semitic backlash, often violent, occurred. For every educational opportunity that opened up, and equally repressive cultural tradition constrained the advance or limited it by gender.

The daughter of a properous Jewish middle-class family, Dora (her real name was Ida Bauer) spent her childhood years surrounded by the illnesses of both of her parents and other adults, and eventually came to define her own life by the illnesses the afflicated her. As the daughter of a liberal Jewish family, the world held for her the promise of education and higher culture, an involvement in social justice and apparently increasingly favorable, if precarious, opportunities for advancement and development both as a Jew and as a female.

That man proposes and God disposes is a generally accepted proposition. Freud, however, being godless, did his own proposing and disposing. He proposed that his private life be kept private, reluctantly exposing—in the service of his scientific formulations in The Interpretation of Dreams and in The Psychopathology of Everyday Life—what he considered far too much of himself. Time and again he destroyed letters, papers, and notes, “mostly to our loss,” Jones, his official biographer, laments. Had it not been for Marie Bonaparte's impassioned and eloquent persuasiveness, he would have had her destroy his letters to Fliess, which she had acquired from an art dealer to whom Ida Fliess, which she had acquired from an art dealer to whom Ida Fliess had sold them after the death of her husband. An Autobiographical Study, written in 1925, is a biography of psychoanalysis rather than of the writer, exposing only as much of its creator as he deemed could reasonably be expected of him and which he could not, in all decency, withhold from his readers. Jones writes that “what he [Freud] revealed of his life was far more carefully selected and censored than is generally supposed.” Yet Freud wrote thousands of letters, their extant number estimated to be between ten and fifteen thousand, making him, according to Mahoney, one of the most prolific letter writers in the history of world literature. And letters, as we know (and as Freud no doubt knew), are disposers par excellence of privacy. Was Freud's unconscious insidiously at work to dispose?

Although Mahler was very satisfied with the initial chapter resulting from her collaboration with the editor of this volume, she “postpond” futher work on the memoir until, as it happened, after her death. Stepansky is tactfully silent, but one tends to suppose that even in her eighties, the material she was working over was still too vivid to be recalled without pain. The very first chapter described how Margaret Mahler's birth, nine months and six days after her parent's marriage, was very much resented by her beautiful, pampered nineteen-year-old mother. Mahler says, “My symbiotic stage of life was difficult: I must have been full of frustrated rage at the rejecting mother whom I greatly loved nonetheless.” When her sister was born, four years later, the mother's maternal instincts were awakened and she greeted the second child with enthusiasm. Mahler says that this was the first infant-mother dyad she studied. Already, before her sister's birth, she had responded to her mother's coldness by becoming quietly observant. “I believe it was my observations of my mother's loving interaction with my sister—and the way it contrasted with her interaction with me—that guided me into pediatrics and psychoanalysis and, more specifically, into my subsequent investigation of the mother-infant dual unity. I do not think it an exaggeration to say that my own mother and sister represented the first mother-child pair that I investigated.”

June Bernstein

June Bernstein

June Bernstein  

The following papers address some frequently raised questions as to the advantages of group over individual analysis, the use of modern psychoanalytic techniques in groups, and what is distinctive about modern analytic group treatment.

Leslie Rosenthal's view of the group as early mother leads him to believe that the deepest issues around constructive and destructive impulses, and the defenses against them, can be aroused and resolved in the group setting. He offers clinical evidence of occasions when patients regressed to early, infantile levels.

William Kirman finds a way to use modern analytic techniques in brief psychotherapy groups. He seeks to provide psychological safety for group members and models a nonattacking form of emotional communication based on Spotnitz's maturational interpretation. Kirman's attitude toward saying what is therapeutic rather than on delivering interpretations that may be true but hurtful is a distinguishing concern of modern analytic group treatment.

Evelyn Liegner offers an example of an entire group in the grip of a single resistance. How she uses her countertransference feelings to respond emotionally demonstrates the successful application of modern analytic techniques in the group setting.

Sidney Love's paper shows how resistance is explored and joined in modern analytic family treatment and how this approach differs from family treatments in which the major decisions about treatment are made by the therapist.

Dolores Welber gives an example of how the modern analytic injunction to say everything operates in a group.

Introductory Perspectives Regarding Countertransference

With the increasing realization that analysis is a very personal experience for the analyst as well as the patient, the analyst's feelings cannot be swept away, nor should they be, by further training analysis as Freud (1910) recommended. Much can be learned about the patient through our countertransference responses. Indeed, in many instances, and this is especially true of patients suffering from relative fixations on primitive mental states, a favorable turn of events which preserves the analytic setting from chaotic collapse may well depend upon the recognition of how a relationship based upon the interaction of transference and countertransference elements recapitulates the repetition compulsion.

Thus, countertransference can be both good and bad for analytic resolution. Obviously, if it is unrecognized, the analyst will lose his analytic orientation, and as Freud (1910) insisted, it will lead to deleterious effects. More often than not the therapist becomes intrusive and subtly blames the patient because the analysis is not proceeding as it should. He may make interpretations that are really criticisms, their purpose aimed at giving the analyst relief rather than furnishing the patient with some insight about his mental processes. In extreme instances the analysis is terminated either because the patient can no longer stand it or the therapist has dismissed the patient because he is too sick and should never have been accepted for treatment in the first place.

The drop-out rate of inner-city high school students causes pain and bewilderment for parents, teachers, and administrators. The youngsters themselves are aware of the self-destructiveness of their behavior and speak about how they “should” get their education, even as they engage in behaviors that ensure they won't.

What the Board of Education attempts to do in this regard has little effect. Traditional training and supervision prescribe that the teacher prepare and impose a controlled agenda, accounting for every class moment. When this fails to keep students goal-oriented and progressing toward achieving a diploma, blame is placed on teachers for not planning well enough, on students for not caring, and on families for neglecting their children. How the teachers are to understand and work effectively with the reality of their students' resistive dynamics is seldom addressed.

To illustrate, at the traditional high school where I taught, youngsters who had failed tenth grade two or more times were placed in “double-holdover” classes. Staff and administration considered work with them a hopeless ordeal. School policy required that this task be rotated, though often it was inflicted on new and unsuspecting teachers or those whom the administration wished to punish. The teacher was expected to survive with a minimum of fuss.

The frustration I felt as a high school English teacher wishing to accomplish the Sisyphean task of keeping all my students in school and engaged in developing themselves led me to seek modern psychoanalytic training.

Lynne Laub

Lynne Laub

Lynne Laub  

Horner describes “being and loving” as an ebb and flow of mutuality in which each person is aware of self and at the same time sensitive to the self of the other. She traces the ability to relate in this way to the foundations laid down in the first three years of life, noting that difficulties in so doing result from derivatives of early conflicts or developmental dilemmas surfacing later in life when the individual attempts to establish an intimate adult relationship. She suggests that the basis of the capacity to love lies in the emotional connection with the mother, who must care for and respond to the child in such a way as to facilitate the establishment of a firm bond of attachment. Without adequate early attachment, healthy separation and individuation cannot take place. Horner argues that most conflicts within relationships result from a fear of loss of self, which she relates to the mother's failure to promote healthy individuation. A person who has been able to attain healthy individuation has the foundation for later security the belief that “I can be myself without losing love.”

Horner fleshes out her theory with clinical examples. She describes how a young boy struggling to attain selfhood and manhood may be thwarted by his mother's interfering with his wish to be separate. His capacity to love women may be damaged by his defensive denial of his need and love for her. Similarly, the girl who attempts to achieve autonomy may be interfered with by a mother who wishes to keep her daughter close to her. As there is less of a cultural demand on girls to become autonomous, the daughter who is discouraged from individuating may stay closer to her mother longer than a son who is treated similarly. Children caught in this bind may come to believe that they have to give up being an individual to keep their mother's love. When, as adults, they shut themselves off from feelings of love and warmth to protect the integrity of the self, they ultimately come to feel deprived and angry. Self-induced deprivation, paradoxically, is the only way they can feel whole.

In 1947 Spotnitz identified certain emotional currents of feeling which operate in the group setting. He identified these as:

The reproductive constellation of forces

The inadequacy constellation of forces

By the reproductive constellation Spotnitz meant those forces that make themselves felt in the desire to have gratifying sex and in the desire to produce a child who will become an adult, healthier and better in every aspect than the parent.

The inadequacy constellation refers to the physical, emotional and integrational inadequacies which deter individuals from the achievement of the ultimate aim of the constellation, i.e., the production of a child who will become a better adult than the parent (Spotnitz, 1947; Spotnitz and Gabriel, 1950).

Spotnitz also identified a third emotional current, the negative reproductive constellation, which referred to those emotional forces which operated in the desire to thwart and prevent sexual gratification and pregnancy, which operated in the desire to produce defective children and to block them from healthy emotional development so that they never in any way become superior to the parent. In treatment these forces are expressed in the treatment-destructive resistances. The most extreme expression of the negative reproductive constellation is seen in the Holocaust.

All these forces can become resistances, i.e., if under the influence of the reproductive constellation, group members set about making babies with each other, or if a whole group encourages two of its members to act out sexually.

To outline the history of modern psychoanalytic training over the last four decades includes the birth and development of modern psychoanalysis itself. But to begin at the very beginning: Freud stated that he considered psychoanalysis to be any line of investigation that takes as its starting point transference and resistance. Most psychoanalysts now would also include the investigation of the countertransference and of emotional communication between patient and analyst, analyst and patient.

Freud and his first followers were pessimistic about psychoanalysis ever being applicable to the study or treatment of what have come to be known as the narcissistic neuroses. Still, Freud seems to have been of the opinion that psychoanalysis would be a living, growing entity as long as someone was interested in it. His position was that psychoanalysis is not a child of speculation, but rather the product of experience, and for that reason unfinished. He invited anyone to study it and to help in its future development. So the door was left open for future researchers to expand the applicability of psychoanalysis, which we have done-particularly, but not only, in the direction of the narcissistic disorders.

The specific body of advances in theory and technique which received the name of modern psychoanalysis arose in the other half of this century, initially as the observations, thoughts, and feelings of one analyst interested in working with schizophrenics. In the mid-1940s, that analyst began to help others to learn to work analyticaly with severely regressed, narcissistic patients. What was born of that effort is now a central current in the mainstream of psychoanalytic theory, practice, and training.

Emanuel Hammer is a Sullivanian psychoanalyst whose call for creativity in therapeutic style is welcome. Elaborating on concepts from his interpersonal orientation, Hammer suggests that artistic participant observation facilitates the empathic and collaborative relationship fundamental to the treatment process. Style is the manner, not the matter, of intervention, and Hammer suggests that it may be essential to therapeutic success. In his experience, when a therapist is open to receiving and imaginatively shaping metaphoric images, and when such artistry is judiciously combined with understanding, emotional awareness and communication are enhanced.

In language, tone, and structure, Hammer's book takes this advice to heart. He avoids jargon and conveys his goal of “reaching the affect” clearly and enthusiastically. Numerous, well-chosen clinical examples illustrate brief discussions of theory. The flexibility and lightness of touch that Hammer advocates come across in his generous descriptions of treatment impasses he has encountered and the stylistic innovations he utilized to resolve them. Chapter organization also carries this message of fluidity and openness, a benefit for time-pressed readers. In addition to presenting his thoughts on the elements of therapeutic style, Hammer makes a case for literary inspiration and elaborates on four specific styles that he terms “poetic,” “earthy,” “creative,” and “playful.” There is also a chapter on the stylistic demands commonly encountered in the treatment of patients with specific disorders.

Repeatedly, Hammer turns to literature as a source of therapeutic learning. Not only are the writer and analyst concerned with the same goals of deepening experience and delivering truth, both also seek to expand the self's realities by means of seeing what others do not see and speaking what others find unspeakable. To illustrate the “converging lines of observation” between therapist, novelist, and patient, Hammer offers entertaining quotations from writers as diverse as Tolstoy, Updike, and Malamud. In his view, analytic technique that provides the patient with, in Fromm-Reichmann's words, “an experience, not an explanation,” should be drawn not so much from texts on transference as from the evocative imagery of the poet.

This paper will be an attempt to clarify the concept of the positive anaclitic countertransference as clinically observed, identified and labelled by Spotnitz in his treatment of patients whose communications remained repetitive despite having undergone long-term analysis.

Let us start with the word anaclitic, which has been familiar to most of us in its use in the term anaclitic depression, characterizing that morbid infant state that occurs when there is premature separation of the infant from its mother. The word is derived from the Greek anaklitos. Freud, in 1914, made reference to the term anlehungstypus in the context of marital choices. The term simply means “a leaning-on type.” In the translation of Freud's works into English, the word was translated as “anaclitic.” The libido, Freud wrote, follows the path of narcissistic needs and attaches itself to objects which ensure satisfaction of those needs. He labelled this choice the anaclitic type, which he distinguished from the narcissistic choice, where the partner is chosen to be as similar to oneself as possible.

In modern psychoanalysis anaclitic is considered synonymous with the adjective “dependent.” Thus all of the narcissistic neuroses and preoedipal disorders, including schizophrenias, have their pathological origins during the stage of childhood when children are completely dependent for growth and nurturance on pregenital love objects, towards whom all their libido is directed.

The method developed by Freud for working with neurotic conditions is fairly straightforward. In a neutral setting, the analyst allows conflicts to be transferred into the clinical relationship. The disappointments and dissatisfactions of the patient's life become a part of that relationship and are put into language. Interpretations are offered to explain how the present is connected with the past, and treatment is concluded when enough has been said so that analyst and patient can part company with predominately positive feelings and the patient has improved his ability to communicate. However, many patients did not respond well to this early psychoanalytic approach.

Since Freud's dismissal of narcissism as untreatable and his portrait of the personality as entrenched “behind the stone wall of narcissism,” analysts have tried to breach that wall in order to make a connection with patients who are withdrawn from the world and detached from their feeling states. Current journal literature records these attempts to make contact with those who live in isolation. Conference titles such as—On Becoming the Patient—are a result of our earnest desire to comprehend how therapeutic influence can occur when regression is to the preobject, or self-object states.

In the Beginning

We know that growth begins with conception and that it takes a mother and father to make a baby. The comfort or discomfort we feel in the womb, the feelings we have, and the sounds we hear even before our birth are the beginnings of our roots as group leaders. So the growth of the modern group analysts begins with their biological conceptions.

In my own case, my mother was a peddler. Both she and my father peddled goods with a wagon, so it's likely I was jostled around. My adjustment to that circumstance was the percursor for later adjustements and leads to the particular way I as a group leader. That's only the beginning. We could go back before our beginnings to the beginnings of our parents. We could go back even further to the beginnings of our grandparents. We're not going to do that. I'm working on what I came into this world with and what is occurring within me and my reactions to the world around me from being in the womb and onward.

In Spotnitz's book The Couch and The Circle (1961), there is a chapter where he focuses on his own early orientation as the oldest brother to his siblings. As arbitrator in charge of guiding their activities, he talkds about the effects of his place in the family and the effects of the particular neighboured he lived in, which was crime-infested.

William Kirman PHD

William Kirman

25 Fifth Avenue

William Kirman   Certified psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City. He is Chairman of Guidance and Counseling at Lond Island Univesity and Director of the Mid Manhattan Institute for Psychoanalysis and Group Therapy. He is the author of Modern Psychoanalysis in the Schools and of numerous articles on countertransference and group therapy.

The similarities between long- and short-term modern analytic group therapy are considerably greater than their differences. Their are, however, a number of concepts and techniques specifically suited to the short-term group that will help the therapist attain optimal progress during the time alloted. It is important to remember that in both long- and short-term modern analytic group therapy the basic goal remains the understaning of transference phenomena and the resolution of resistances that impede positive interpersonal communication.

My experience over the years in teaching psychology and group dynamics classses at the college level has helped me to evolve, first, a way of making the academic classroom experience a therapeutic one (Kirman, 1977), and then a way of making the experience into actual short-term group therapy within the college semester. In addition, a number of short-term therapy groups concducted in a clinical setting have helped me to crystallize and generalize basic concepts relating to the short-term group experience.

Historically, the early work with groups either had limited goals, as in Pratt's (1907) tubercular patients where the groups were an adjunct to medical managment, or the groups themselves were slated for a brief period of time. The idea of long-term, ongoing group therapy took some time to evolve.

It was alfred Adler (1930), somewhat later, who saw the value of groups for educational purposes. He gave demonstrations of counseling students while teachers, social workers and doctors observed the process—not quite group therapy, but the beginnings of recognition that learning can be enhanced by socal interaction.

Sometimes, even though the patient is operating on a regressed level, it may be beneficial to utilize the positive anaclitic countertransferential feelings of the analyst in order to resolve resistances to maturation. Spotnitz (1983) describes these as “those feelings the patient needed to become a mature adult but did not get (the missing feelings).” The anaclitic countertransference evolves de novo only from a long-term relationship with the patient and comes about as a product of that relationship … the feelings turn out to be the very feelings of which the patient was deprived during his dependent years, yet were needed for his maturation. These feelings are not induced from the past … The anaclitic feelings have no connection with the patient's prior experience nor with the analyst's subjective history” (Liegner, 1991). In other words, the anaclitic countertransference reflects those feelings which the analyst experiences as a result of her own personality development in the face of a long-term relationship with another person. There is an evolution of interdependency which always occurs between humans when they experience feelings, which communicate the intrinsic value of one person to another.

I would like to report the usefulness of this theoretical approach as it was demonstrated in a group setting where the analyst's induced feelings and those of the other group members were used to catalyze an anaclitic maturational experience in two group members.

The group from which these examples are drawn is a male/female group that has been together in various incarnations for about 14 years. Currently there are sixteen members: six have been together more than 10 years, eight longer than 8 years, and two about 5 years.

Gerald Fishbein

Gerald Fishbein  

Reading this book could be a worthwhile challenge to modern analysts. It is heavily philosophical, highly scholarly, influenced by the writer's extensive scientific training and experience and, ultimately, might provide modern psychoanalysts with a more solid foundation of theory for our technical work with patients than any other psychoanalytic theory.

Robert Holt, an internationally known Freud scholar, who has himself been challenging psychoanalytic theoreticians over the past three decades, has written a comprehensive and authoritative critique of the fundamental theory of psychoanalysis. The book jacket informs us that “it is more comprehensive than other works on Freud's attempts to construct a scientific theory and more systematic in its consideration of all aspects of metapsychology; and that it will be required reading for all serious students of psychoanalytic theory. Beginning students will find that it explains and clarifies much of what is mystifying and difficult to understand in Feud's work, while the most advanced scholars will be challenged to take a position on Holt's call for fundamental reform.”

Holt introduces the book with a reference to Erich Fromm. Holt says, “Erich Fromm once remarked, in a seminar I attended over 40 years ago, that Freud and Marx had this in common: both were the indispensable starting point for students of their respective subject matters, although practically everything they said was wrong.” Such is the dramatic hyperbole of Holt's book. Yet, the reader must feel the deep love and admiration Holt feels for Freud. Holt writes:

And yet Freud is much more than an historical figure. Again, Fromm was right: he is the indispensable starting point for any serious student of psychoanalysis or psychotherapy … not as a source of infalliable wisdom, for there is none such to be found anywhere; not as an intellectual father to be swallowed whole in a fantasied act of magical identification; and not as a generator of propositions that can be carried directly to the laboratory for rigorous verification or falsification.
